meta.title: Samsung Electronics — Lee Jae-yong's memory-and-foundry conglomerate through the HBM and AI server cycle
meta.abstract: Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd. is a South Korean multinational electronics company listed on the Korea Exchange (KRX: 005930) and is the largest constituent of the Samsung Group conglomerate. Headquartered in Suwon, South Korea, Samsung Electronics operates four reporting business divisions: Device Solutions (Memory plus Foundry plus System LSI plus broader semiconductor); Device eXperience (Mobile Experience including Galaxy smartphones, Visual Display, Digital Appliances, broader consumer electronics); Harman (Connected Car and broader automotive electronics through the Harman International subsidiary acquired in 2017); and broader supporting business activities. The corporate trajectory through 2014-2026 has been substantially shaped by the multi-generational Lee family leadership succession (Lee Kun-hee 1987-2014, Lee Jae-yong de facto since 2014 and Executive Chairman since 2022), the multi-decade transformation of Samsung Electronics into one of the largest global semiconductor and consumer electronics companies, and more recent strategic positioning toward the AI infrastructure cycle through the HBM (high bandwidth memory) supply to Nvidia and the broader AI server customer category. The fiscal 2024 revenue was approximately KRW 300.9 trillion (~USD 226 billion) reflecting the broader business division trajectory. The memory business positioning across DRAM and NAND plus the HBM growth driver supporting the AI infrastructure cycle provides the principal recent forward strategic context.

chapters.body:
## The HBM Turn

Samsung Electronics' AI-era inflection point had been the recovery of its memory franchise at the precise moment high-bandwidth memory became the bottleneck inside accelerated computing systems. Samsung said in February 2024 that it had developed the industry's first 36GB 12-high HBM3E device, with bandwidth of up to 1,280GB per second, and in its first-quarter 2024 results it said it had begun mass production of 8-high HBM3E in April and was preparing 12-high mass production in the second quarter. By the third quarter of 2025, management said HBM3E was in mass production and being sold to all related customers. In February 2026 Samsung said it had begun commercial shipment of HBM4, rated at 11.7Gbps and up to 3.3TB per second per stack, and in first-quarter 2026 results it said the Memory business had already recorded the industry's first mass-product sales of HBM4 and SOCAMM2 for NVIDIA's Vera Rubin platform. [HBM3E 12H](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-develops-industry-first-36gb-hbm3e-12h-dram>), [Q1 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2024-results>), [Q3 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-third-quarter-2025-results>), [HBM4 shipment](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-ships-industry-first-commercial-hbm4-with-ultimate-performance-for-ai-computing>), [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

That sequence mattered because it replaced the earlier, weakly sourced account of an 18-month qualification purgatory with what Samsung itself had actually disclosed by the frozen window: a 2024 HBM3E build-out, a 2025 move into commercial customer shipments and a 2026 shift into HBM4 revenue. It still left open the question of share and allocation versus SK Hynix and Micron, but it meant Samsung was no longer absent from the highest-value memory tier. The company described the business in 2025 and early 2026 less as a turnaround story than as a portfolio upgrade, with HBM, server DDR5, GDDR7 and enterprise SSDs taking a larger share of mix. [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>), [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

## Corporate Frame

Samsung Electronics, incorporated in 1969 and renamed Samsung Electronics Co. Ltd. in 1984, remained the flagship operating company of the Samsung Group. Jay Y. Lee was formally appointed Executive Chairman in October 2022, codifying the succession that had in practice begun after Lee Kun-hee's incapacitation in 2014. The company's earnings materials and corporate fact sheets described a portfolio spanning Device Solutions, Device eXperience, Samsung Display and HARMAN, with HARMAN preserved as a distinct subsidiary after Samsung completed the acquisition in March 2017 at $112 a share in cash. [IR general information](<https://www.samsung.com/global/ir/ir-resources/faq/>), [Jay Y. Lee appointment](<https://news.samsung.com/global/jay-y-lee-appointed-samsung-electronics-executive-chairman>), [Fast Facts](<https://news.samsung.com/global/fast-facts>), [HARMAN close](<https://news.samsung.com/us/samsung-electronics-completes-acquisition-of-harman>)

The industrial logic of the group was still the same one Samsung had spent decades constructing: memory and logic at one end, branded consumer hardware at the other, and a growing automotive and components layer in between. What changed in the frozen-window period was not the basic map of the conglomerate but the hierarchy of profit drivers. Through 2023 the memory crash had overwhelmed the rest of the portfolio. By 2025 and into the first quarter of 2026, semiconductors again dominated the earnings picture.

## Financial Scale

The headline financial record through the frozen window was as follows:

| Period | Revenue (KRW tn) | Operating profit (KRW tn) |
|---|---:|---:|
| FY2022 | 302.23 | 43.38 |
| FY2023 | 258.94 | 6.57 |
| FY2024 | 300.9 | 32.7 |
| FY2025 | 333.6 | 43.6 |
| Q1 2026 | 133.9 | 57.2 |

The 2023 trough had been real, but so had the rebound. Fiscal 2025 set a new annual revenue record at KRW 333.6 trillion, and the first quarter of 2026 alone generated KRW 57.2 trillion of operating profit, exceeding the company's full-year 2025 operating profit. That was not a typo in the dossier and did not need softening; it was the figure Samsung itself reported. [FY 2022 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2022-results>), [FY 2023 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2023-results>), [FY 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2024-results>), [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>), [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

The divisional swing was even sharper. In the fourth quarter of 2025 the Device Solutions division produced KRW 44.0 trillion of revenue and KRW 16.4 trillion of operating profit. In the first quarter of 2026 DS revenue rose to KRW 81.7 trillion and operating profit to KRW 53.7 trillion, driven by what Samsung described as technological leadership in memory and higher average selling prices. Device eXperience, by contrast, remained large but far less lucrative: Q1 2026 DX revenue was KRW 38.1 trillion and operating profit KRW 2.8 trillion. [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>), [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

## Foundry and Mobile After HBM

The rest of the investment case still mattered because Samsung was not just a memory supplier. In June 2022 it became the first foundry to begin chip production on a 3nm process using gate-all-around architecture, and at Samsung Foundry Forum 2024 it extended the roadmap around SF2 and later nodes while pushing a one-stop pitch that paired foundry, packaging and memory. In July 2024 it also announced a 2nm GAA plus advanced packaging deal with Preferred Networks for AI accelerators, a useful primary-source confirmation that Samsung's foundry business was still winning named advanced-node work even as the market remained structurally tilted toward TSMC. [3nm GAA production](<https://news.samsung.com/us/samsung-begins-chip-production-3nm-process-gaa-architecture>), [SFF 2024](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-showcases-ai-era-vision-and-latest-foundry-technologies-at-sff-2024>), [Preferred Networks](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-to-provide-turnkey-semiconductor-solutions-with-2nm-gaa-process-and-2-5d-package-to-preferred-networks>)

On the consumer side, the company's mobile narrative had shifted from unit volume to AI-led premium retention. Samsung introduced the Galaxy S24 series in January 2024 as the opening move in its "mobile AI" campaign, and by fiscal 2025 it said the Galaxy S24 family had delivered double-digit full-year growth while the Q1 2026 launch cycle centred on new flagship smartphones. The dossier's earlier claims about exact 2025 S25 growth rates and channel data had not been supportable from primary sources, so they were removed in favour of what Samsung actually disclosed: strong flagship mix, AI positioning and a DX business that was still profitable but secondary to the semiconductor rebound. [Galaxy S24 launch](<https://news.samsung.com/global/enter-the-new-era-of-mobile-ai-with-samsung-galaxy-s24-series>), [FY 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2024-results>), [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>), [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

The corrected picture was therefore more defensible and, if anything, more striking. Samsung had entered the frozen window as a company whose semiconductor engine had re-asserted itself with unusual force, whose HBM gap had narrowed enough to produce real 2025 and 2026 disclosures, and whose consumer and automotive franchises remained important but no longer central to the earnings story. The strategic question was not whether Samsung had scale. It was whether the company could keep translating that scale into the specific high-performance memory and leading-edge logic products the AI build-out rewarded most richly.

chapters.title: From 1969 founding through Lee Kun-hee, IMF crisis, Lee Jae-yong succession
chapters.body:
## Origins in the House of Samsung

Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd. was incorporated on 13 January 1969 in Suwon, South Korea, as the electronics manufacturing arm of the Samsung Group conglomerate founded three decades earlier by Lee Byung-chul. The parent group had operated as a trading company, insurance business, and sugar refiner before Lee Byung-chul identified consumer electronics — television sets, washing machines, calculators — as the industry most likely to generate the foreign-exchange earnings a capital-starved, export-dependent Korea required. Samsung Electronics' first products were black-and-white television sets assembled under licence from Japanese manufacturers; its first television rolled off the Suwon line in 1970. The founding premise was not technological originality but disciplined manufacturing scale deployed in service of national industrialisation — a logic that would define Samsung's competitive posture for the following two decades and whose structural echoes remain visible across the company's semiconductor and foundry operations today.

The transition from licensed assembly to proprietary manufacture was gradual and deliberate. Throughout the 1970s Samsung Electronics expanded its consumer product range — colour televisions followed in 1977, microwave ovens in 1979 — while investing in what were then modest but strategically significant engineering teams. The decisive pivot came in 1983, when Lee Byung-chul announced Samsung's entry into DRAM semiconductor production. The decision was widely criticised at the time: Samsung possessed neither the intellectual property, the process engineering, nor the customer relationships that American and Japanese memory manufacturers had accumulated over years. Lee Byung-chul proceeded regardless, authorising capital expenditure that was, relative to Samsung Electronics' then-revenues, an act of corporate faith. A 64K DRAM chip was produced in Seoul in November 1983, six months after development work commenced — a pace that surprised industry observers and established the template of compressed development timelines that Samsung would sustain for the next four decades.

## The Kun-hee Chairmanship and the Frankfurt Declaration

Lee Byung-chul died in November 1987. His third son, Lee Kun-hee, assumed the chairmanship of Samsung Group later that year, inheriting a conglomerate that was large by Korean standards but not yet a credible global technology company. Lee Kun-hee spent the first years of his tenure observing the gap — in quality, design, brand, and engineering — between Samsung's products and those of Sony, Motorola, and the Japanese memory majors. His conclusion was uncomfortable: Samsung had scaled volume without building the qualitative foundations on which durable competitive advantage rested.

The resulting strategic intervention, delivered in June 1993 at a gathering of senior Samsung managers in Frankfurt, Germany, entered Korean corporate history as the Frankfurt Declaration. Lee Kun-hee's instruction to the assembled executives was unambiguous: ["Change everything except your wife and children."](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-innovation-forum-kicks-off-in-korea>) Samsung would halt production — including, symbolically, the destruction of inventory — and rebuild its quality-control and engineering culture from first principles. Products that failed inspection were burned in public at the Gumi plant in 1995. The Frankfurt Declaration was not merely a quality initiative; it was a signal about the kind of company Samsung intended to become. Within five years, the outcome was legible: Samsung's DRAM market position had moved from a fast-follower to a technology-and-cost leader, and the company's brand was beginning to command premium pricing in export markets.

## Memory Supremacy and the 1990s DRAM Decade

Samsung's ascent in DRAM was the defining industrial story of the 1990s semiconductor cycle. By the mid-1990s Samsung had displaced Japanese manufacturers — NEC, Hitachi, Fujitsu — to become the world's largest DRAM producer by volume, a position it retained without interruption through the frozen-window date. The competitive mechanism was straightforward in principle and exceptionally demanding in execution: Samsung invested through cycles while competitors retrenched, which compressed its cost curve while peers were managing balance sheets. When memory prices collapsed in the cyclical downturns of 1995–1996, Samsung's stronger cash position allowed continued capital expenditure; when prices recovered, Samsung entered the upturn with newer fabs and lower unit costs than its rivals.

The NAND flash business followed a similar arc. Samsung introduced commercial NAND flash production in 1992 and scaled aggressively through the late 1990s and 2000s as the market for portable consumer electronics — cameras, MP3 players, and eventually smartphones — created structural demand growth. By the mid-2000s Samsung was the world's largest NAND flash producer. The accumulated memory expertise provided the manufacturing-process and yield-engineering culture on which subsequent HBM ambitions would be built — though, as later chapters address, that heritage did not prevent a significant qualification lag against SK Hynix on the AI-infrastructure HBM demand cycle.

## The IMF Crisis and Chaebol Reckoning

The Asian Financial Crisis that struck South Korea with full force in November 1997 — triggering the International Monetary Fund's then-record $57 billion bailout package — tested the chaebol structure of which Samsung Electronics was the most prominent constituent. The Korean government's precondition for IMF support included demands for chaebol restructuring: debt reduction, affiliate disposal, and a scaling back of the cross-guarantees that had allowed member companies within groups to leverage each other's balance sheets into systemic fragility. The crisis forced the large chaebol groups to cut leverage and dispose of non-core assets, and Samsung responded by narrowing capital allocation around businesses where it already had scale and export competitiveness.

Samsung Electronics navigated the crisis with greater agility than many peers. Lee Kun-hee oversaw the disposal of affiliates including Samsung Motor — sold to Renault in 2000 in what became Renault Korea — and concentrated capital allocation on the semiconductor and electronics businesses where Samsung possessed genuine competitive standing. The memory business proved particularly well-suited to crisis management: DRAM and NAND flash were globally traded commodities for which Samsung held a cost-structure advantage regardless of domestic Korean economic conditions. Revenue derived in US dollars provided a partial natural hedge against the won's sharp depreciation. By 2000, Samsung Electronics had returned to profitability and resumed capital investment. The IMF episode reinforced the concentration on a smaller number of globally competitive businesses that Lee Kun-hee had begun telegraphing with the Frankfurt Declaration.

## The Mobile Decade and Galaxy's Rise

Samsung Electronics entered the mobile handset business in the early 1990s, initially producing handsets for foreign network operators under original design manufacturer arrangements. The smartphone era, which Apple's first iPhone inaugurated in June 2007, initially appeared to threaten Samsung's feature-phone scale position. Samsung's response was the Galaxy S series, launched in June 2010 on the Android platform, which within three years had made Samsung the world's largest smartphone manufacturer by unit volume — a position it held continuously thereafter. The Galaxy S and subsequently the Galaxy Note series demonstrated that a Korean manufacturer with deep display, memory, and processor integration capabilities could compete on product experience against Cupertino's hardware-software integration.

The mobile success carried its own internal logic: because Samsung manufactured the AMOLED displays, DRAM and NAND memory, and Exynos application processors inside its Galaxy devices, vertical integration provided both cost advantages and a design-to-manufacturing feedback loop. The Galaxy business also created a direct branded relationship with hundreds of millions of consumers in markets — India, Southeast Asia, Latin America — where Apple's premium pricing limited its penetration. By the peak of its mobile dominance in the early 2010s, Samsung's mobile division contributed the majority of group operating profit.

## The Succession: From Kun-hee to Jae-yong

Lee Kun-hee suffered a heart attack on 10 May 2014 and was hospitalised in a condition that left him incapacitated as an executive. His son, Lee Jae-yong — known internationally as Jay Y. Lee — had been serving as Vice Chairman since 2012 following a structured career progression through Samsung Group affiliate roles from 1991. The father's incapacitation accelerated the de facto transfer of group leadership that had been proceeding by gradual design. By the second half of 2014 Lee Jae-yong was exercising the operational and strategic authority of the Samsung Group chairmanship, meeting government officials, managing supplier and customer relationships, and directing capital allocation decisions across the group's constituent businesses.

The formal succession was delayed by legal proceedings. Lee Jae-yong was arrested in February 2017 in connection with bribery allegations arising from Samsung's payments to foundations connected to then-President Park Geun-hye, whose subsequent impeachment and removal became one of the defining political events of contemporary Korea. Lee was convicted in 2017, released on appeal, and ultimately received a presidential pardon in August 2022. The legal proceedings consumed years of executive attention and constrained Samsung's ability to pursue significant transactions requiring concentrated leadership bandwidth — a period during which competitors including TSMC continued accelerating advanced-node investment and SK Hynix was deepening the high-bandwidth memory engineering partnerships that would later crystallise into the HBM3E NVIDIA qualification lead.

Lee Kun-hee died on 25 October 2020. His death formally vacated the Samsung Electronics Chairman title and triggered the inheritance proceedings on what was, by Korean tax authority assessment, one of the largest personal estates in Korean history — estimated at approximately KRW 26 trillion at time of death, with inheritance taxes requiring multi-year payments. In October 2022, Samsung's board formally appointed Lee Jae-yong as Executive Chairman of Samsung Electronics, completing a succession that had been in operational fact underway since 2014 and in de jure process since Lee Kun-hee's death two years prior.

## Harman and the Diversification Logic

One notable strategic action executed under Lee Jae-yong's de facto leadership was the November 2016 announcement of the acquisition of Harman International Industries for approximately $8 billion — Samsung Electronics' largest acquisition to that point. Harman's portfolio included the JBL, Harman Kardon, and AKG audio brands together with a substantial automotive infotainment and connected-vehicle systems business. The strategic rationale was explicit: Samsung sought a hardware-plus-software wedge into the automotive electronics market ahead of the anticipated convergence of connectivity, electrification, and in-vehicle computing. The transaction closed in March 2017 and Harman was retained as a distinct subsidiary. By the frozen window, HARMAN remained Samsung Electronics' primary automotive-technology platform, still run as a distinct subsidiary after the March 2017 close. [Samsung HARMAN close](<https://news.samsung.com/us/samsung-electronics-completes-acquisition-of-harman>)
