chapters.body:
## The Operating Map Behind the Conglomerate

Samsung Electronics did not report itself as a simple consumer-electronics group with a semiconductor adjunct. By the frozen window, the company's quarterly materials consistently broke the business into Device Solutions, Device eXperience, Samsung Display Corporation and HARMAN, with corporate and intercompany items bridging the consolidated statements. That mattered because the dossier's earlier segment narrative overstated simplicity and imported secondary-source market-share claims that were not needed to understand how Samsung actually made money. [Fast Facts](<https://news.samsung.com/global/fast-facts>), [FY 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2024-results>), [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>), [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

## Device Solutions: The Earnings Engine Again

Device Solutions contained the memory business, foundry and System LSI, and it had returned to being the company's economic centre of gravity. In the fourth quarter of 2024 DS posted KRW 30.1 trillion of revenue and KRW 2.9 trillion of operating profit. A year later, in the fourth quarter of 2025, DS revenue had climbed to KRW 44.0 trillion and operating profit to KRW 16.4 trillion as HBM, server DDR5 and enterprise SSD demand tightened supply. In the first quarter of 2026 the division generated KRW 81.7 trillion of revenue and KRW 53.7 trillion of operating profit, an extraordinary jump driven by memory pricing, mix and the first revenue contribution from HBM4. [FY 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2024-results>), [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>), [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

Within DS, Memory remained the dominant profit pool. Samsung's official commentary through 2024-2026 repeatedly centred on HBM, DDR5, LPDDR5X, GDDR7 and enterprise SSDs rather than commodity DRAM alone. The company said the Memory business had begun mass production of 8-high HBM3E in April 2024, developed a 36GB 12-high HBM3E part in February 2024, moved HBM3E into sales to related customers by the third quarter of 2025 and started commercial HBM4 shipments in February 2026. That sequence anchored the division's rebound more clearly than any external estimate of share could have done. [HBM3E 12H](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-develops-industry-first-36gb-hbm3e-12h-dram>), [Q1 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2024-results>), [Q3 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-third-quarter-2025-results>), [HBM4 shipment](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-ships-industry-first-commercial-hbm4-with-ultimate-performance-for-ai-computing>), [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

Samsung's own year-end 2024 disclosure also made the portfolio shift more concrete. Management said the Memory business was accelerating migration to the 1b-nm process in DRAM, increasing the share of DDR5 and LPDDR5X shipments, moving NAND from V6 to V8 and expanding V7 QLC-based server SSD sales. The point was not merely that DS sold memory. It was that the company was deliberately tilting the segment toward higher-density and higher-value products whose economics looked meaningfully better than those of legacy DRAM and commodity NAND. [FY 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2024-results>)

The foundry and System LSI businesses sat inside the same division but followed a different cadence. Samsung had been first to 3nm GAA production in June 2022, yet management's own disclosures showed that leading-edge foundry remained a work in progress rather than a solved profit centre. In fiscal 2024 the company said it would focus on stabilising 2nm GAA and strengthening the 4nm design infrastructure. In the third quarter of 2025 it said the Foundry business had achieved record-high customer orders, mainly on advanced nodes, and had started mass production of first-generation 2nm GAA. In the first quarter of 2026 it said the business would pursue large-scale 2nm orders while continuing 1.4nm R&D. [3nm GAA production](<https://news.samsung.com/us/samsung-begins-chip-production-3nm-process-gaa-architecture>), [FY 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2024-results>), [Q3 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-third-quarter-2025-results>), [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

## Device eXperience: Large, Durable, Less Profitable

Device eXperience combined mobile, televisions, digital appliances and the networks business. It was not a small appendage: Samsung reported KRW 38.1 trillion of DX revenue and KRW 2.8 trillion of operating profit in the first quarter of 2026. But compared with DS, DX had become the stabiliser rather than the decisive earnings driver. [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

The mobile arm within DX remained strategically important because it preserved Samsung's premium consumer brand and created internal demand for displays, memory and, where applicable, Exynos silicon. Samsung launched the Galaxy S24 family in January 2024 as the opening of the Galaxy AI cycle. In fiscal 2024 it said the Galaxy S24 series had delivered double-digit full-year growth, and in fiscal 2025 it positioned the Galaxy S26 launch around "Agentic AI experiences" and slimmer, lighter flagship form factors. The earlier dossier had imported external unit estimates and channel checks; the primary-source version was cleaner and more reliable. Samsung itself documented premium flagship growth, AI-led positioning and the continued importance of tablets and wearables to mix. [Galaxy S24 launch](<https://news.samsung.com/global/enter-the-new-era-of-mobile-ai-with-samsung-galaxy-s24-series>), [FY 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2024-results>), [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>)

The quarterly mix inside DX also deserved more precision than the old draft gave it. In the fourth quarter of 2024, Samsung said the MX and Networks businesses generated KRW 25.8 trillion of revenue and KRW 2.1 trillion of operating profit. In the fourth quarter of 2025, the same grouping delivered KRW 29.3 trillion of revenue and KRW 1.9 trillion of operating profit, with management emphasising that the MX business had still achieved double-digit annual profit for the year despite the normalisation of launch effects. That is a more useful way to think about DX than broad unit-leadership rhetoric: mobile remained profitable and strategically important, but its contribution had become bounded relative to DS. [FY 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2024-results>), [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>)

DX also contained Visual Display and Digital Appliances, whose earnings were materially more cyclical than the brand strength sometimes suggested. In the fourth quarter of 2025 the VD and DA businesses posted KRW 14.8 trillion of revenue and a KRW 0.6 trillion operating loss as market competition remained intense and seasonal appliance demand softened. Samsung's own guidance for 2026 therefore leaned on premium TV mix, AI appliances, HVAC growth and operational efficiency rather than any claim that televisions or refrigerators would re-take the group's profit crown. [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>)

## Samsung Display: Separate Disclosure, Strategic Importance

Samsung Display Corporation was disclosed separately in earnings materials rather than folded invisibly into DX. That treatment was important because display economics did not always move in lockstep with the handset cycle. SDC posted KRW 8.1 trillion of revenue and KRW 0.9 trillion of operating profit in the fourth quarter of 2024, KRW 9.5 trillion and KRW 2.0 trillion respectively in the fourth quarter of 2025, and KRW 6.7 trillion of revenue with KRW 0.4 trillion of operating profit in the first quarter of 2026. The business described itself as maintaining premium leadership through differentiated smartphone displays, QD-OLED monitors and large-panel products, but the figures showed a contributor rather than a group-level driver. [FY 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2024-results>), [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>), [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

Those numbers also mattered strategically. SDC gave Samsung a second advanced-component business whose cycles were not identical to those of memory. That did not make the company immune to semiconductor volatility, but it did help explain why Samsung could keep premium handset and monitor propositions differentiated even when foundry or commodity-memory conditions were weaker.

## HARMAN: Automotive Platform, Still Distinct

HARMAN remained a distinct reporting lens nearly a decade after the acquisition closed. Samsung completed the deal in March 2017 for $112 per share in cash and kept the business as a standalone subsidiary. In the fourth quarter of 2025 HARMAN posted KRW 4.6 trillion of revenue and KRW 0.3 trillion of operating profit, supported by automotive product supply to European OEMs and new portable-audio launches. Samsung's first-quarter 2026 commentary said HARMAN earnings had declined because of higher expenses, memory constraints and audio seasonality, but the strategic role was unchanged: digital cockpit, car audio and adjacent automotive electronics remained Samsung's most direct non-handset route into the vehicle stack. [HARMAN close](<https://news.samsung.com/us/samsung-electronics-completes-acquisition-of-harman>), [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>), [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

## What the Structure Meant

The corrected segment picture made two things clear. First, Samsung's diversification was real: few companies simultaneously ran top-tier memory fabs, a global smartphone franchise, a major display subsidiary and an automotive-electronics platform. Second, diversification did not make the earnings engine symmetrical. Through the frozen window, profits were again being made overwhelmingly in semiconductors. DX, SDC and HARMAN mattered because they broadened the franchise, softened some cycles and supplied strategic optionality. DS mattered because it determined the slope of the income statement.

chapters.title: Revenue trajectory, memory cycle, HBM economics, Foundry margins
chapters.body:
## The Cycle in the Numbers

Samsung Electronics' financial record from 2020 through the frozen window read like a condensed history of the electronics and memory cycle. Revenue rose from KRW 236.81 trillion in 2020 to KRW 279.6 trillion in 2021 and KRW 302.23 trillion in 2022, then fell back to KRW 258.94 trillion in 2023 before recovering to KRW 300.9 trillion in 2024 and a new annual record of KRW 333.6 trillion in 2025. The sharper story sat in operating profit, which moved from KRW 35.99 trillion in 2020 to KRW 51.63 trillion in 2021, down to KRW 43.38 trillion in 2022, then collapsed to KRW 6.57 trillion in 2023 before recovering to KRW 32.7 trillion in 2024 and KRW 43.6 trillion in 2025. [FY 2020 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2020-results>), [FY 2021 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2021-results>), [FY 2022 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2022-results>), [FY 2023 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2023-results>), [FY 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2024-results>), [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>)

| Period | Revenue (KRW tn) | Operating profit (KRW tn) |
|---|---:|---:|
| FY2020 | 236.81 | 35.99 |
| FY2021 | 279.6 | 51.63 |
| FY2022 | 302.23 | 43.38 |
| FY2023 | 258.94 | 6.57 |
| FY2024 | 300.9 | 32.7 |
| FY2025 | 333.6 | 43.6 |
| Q1 2026 | 133.9 | 57.2 |

The first quarter of 2026 deserves separate emphasis because the number looked implausible until checked against Samsung's own release. The company reported KRW 133.9 trillion of quarterly revenue and KRW 57.2 trillion of operating profit, both record figures. That meant the first quarter of 2026 alone produced more operating profit than the whole of fiscal 2025. [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

## The 2023 Drawdown Was a Semiconductor Event

The dossier's earlier draft had correctly characterised 2023 as the trough, but some of the supporting detail had been thinly sourced. Samsung's official filings make the point more precisely. In first-quarter 2023 the group reported KRW 63.75 trillion of revenue and only KRW 0.64 trillion of operating profit, with the DS division posting KRW 13.73 trillion of revenue and KRW 4.58 trillion of operating losses. By year-end, the official 2023 fourth-quarter interim report showed the DS segment at a full-year operating loss of KRW 14.8795 trillion. That was the centre of gravity of the downturn: not a broad consumer collapse across every business line, but a semiconductor drawdown large enough to swamp the rest of the company. [Q1 2023 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2023-results>), [2023 4Q interim report](<https://images.samsung.com/is/content/samsung/assets/global/ir/docs/2023_4Q_Interim_Report.pdf>), [FY 2023 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2023-results>)

The same official filings also help explain why the company did not collapse outright. The 2023 fourth-quarter interim report showed DX still profitable on a full-year basis, which meant the device businesses continued to throw off earnings even as DS fell deeply into loss. The lesson was not that diversification neutralised the cycle. It was that diversification bought Samsung time while the memory and foundry businesses absorbed the downturn.

The quarterly pattern during the trough fits that view. First-quarter 2023 was the nadir. Through the middle of the year management kept talking about weak demand, inventory adjustment and a gradual second-half recovery. By the fourth quarter of 2023 it was already reporting that the DRAM business had returned to profit, that inventories were depleting and that HBM, DDR5, LPDDR5X and UFS 4.0 sales had increased. The rebound did not come because Samsung discovered a new business model; it came because pricing, mix and utilisation in memory turned.

## 2024 Recovery, But Not Yet Cleanly Balanced

Fiscal 2024 restored scale faster than profitability. Annual revenue returned to KRW 300.9 trillion, the second-highest on record, and operating profit recovered to KRW 32.7 trillion. Yet fourth-quarter 2024 operating profit was only KRW 6.5 trillion, down quarter-on-quarter because market conditions stayed soft for IT products and spending on R&D increased. The DS division posted KRW 30.1 trillion of revenue and KRW 2.9 trillion of operating profit in that quarter, evidence of a recovery, but not yet of the full earnings force that would show up later. [FY 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2024-results>)

That is the right way to read 2024: as the bridge year. Samsung's memory business said HBM and high-density DDR5 for servers had pushed the fourth-quarter blended DRAM average selling price higher, but it was also absorbing initial ramp-up costs to secure production capacity for cutting-edge nodes. Meanwhile System LSI earnings were hurt by weak mobile demand and higher R&D, and the company was explicit that it would keep spending to secure technology leadership rather than optimise for near-term margin. Management also laid out the concrete mechanics of the mix shift, including faster migration to the 1b-nm process, higher DDR5 and LPDDR5X exposure and the expansion of QLC server SSD sales. [FY 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2024-results>)

Samsung Display and HARMAN also underscored the incomplete nature of the rebound. Both contributed positively in the period, but neither was large enough to change the central truth of the income statement: until DS normalised, the group could not look normalised.

## 2025 and Early 2026 Repriced the Whole Group

By 2025 the operating leverage of the recovery had become much more obvious. Samsung reported KRW 93.8 trillion of revenue and KRW 20.1 trillion of operating profit in the fourth quarter of 2025, at that point both all-time highs. The DS division alone generated KRW 44.0 trillion of revenue and KRW 16.4 trillion of operating profit, and the company said R&D spending reached a full-year record of KRW 37.7 trillion. The signal from management was not that the investment phase was ending, but that it was being funded from a much stronger earnings base. [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>)

First-quarter 2026 then pushed the numbers to an extreme few analysts would have pencilled in two years earlier. DS revenue rose to KRW 81.7 trillion and operating profit to KRW 53.7 trillion. Samsung attributed the move to technological leadership in memory and higher ASPs, while also noting that DX had remained profitable at KRW 2.8 trillion. The asymmetry underscored the point made elsewhere in the dossier: Samsung was again being valued through semiconductors first and everything else second. [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

## Capital Intensity Never Went Away

The recovery was not achieved by shrinking the industrial base. Samsung's capital expenditures were KRW 53.1 trillion in 2023, KRW 53.6 trillion in 2024, and the company kept emphasising advanced-node migration, packaging and capacity preparation. In 2024 alone, KRW 46.3 trillion of capex went to DS and KRW 4.8 trillion to SDC. This mattered because it explained why earnings could recover so violently once pricing and mix improved: Samsung had preserved and continued expanding the manufacturing system that the downturn had temporarily made look excessive. [FY 2023 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2023-results>), [FY 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2024-results>)

Another way to state the same point is that Samsung's financial shape by the frozen window had become more concentrated even as the group stayed diversified in form. SDC, HARMAN and DX all contributed, but the decisive change in the model came from semiconductors: better pricing, better mix and a more commercially relevant HBM position than the company had in 2023 or early 2024. That is why the first-quarter 2026 earnings release read so differently from the 2023 trough materials despite coming from the same corporate perimeter.

The corrected reading, then, was less melodramatic than the earlier draft and more consequential. Samsung did not move from collapse to redemption because external commentary changed tone. It moved because the memory cycle turned, high-value products became a larger share of output, and the company entered 2026 with an earnings profile once again dominated by semiconductors rather than defended by conglomerate diversification.

chapters.title: Post-Kun-hee era through Lee Jae-yong, memory cycles, HBM challenge
chapters.body:
## Memory's Collapse and Return

The earnings story of the Lee Jae-yong period was not a straight line of succession-era consolidation. It was a severe semiconductor drawdown followed by a rapid repricing of the same business once AI memory demand tightened the market. Samsung's own releases showed revenue at KRW 302.23 trillion in 2022, KRW 258.94 trillion in 2023, KRW 300.9 trillion in 2024 and KRW 333.6 trillion in 2025. Operating profit fell much harder, from KRW 43.38 trillion in 2022 to KRW 6.57 trillion in 2023, before recovering to KRW 32.7 trillion in 2024 and KRW 43.6 trillion in 2025. [FY 2022 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2022-results>), [FY 2023 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2023-results>), [FY 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2024-results>), [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>)

The trough was concentrated in Device Solutions. In first-quarter 2023 Samsung reported only KRW 0.64 trillion of group operating profit, with the DS division posting KRW 4.58 trillion of operating losses. The official 2023 fourth-quarter interim report then showed DS at a full-year operating loss of KRW 14.8795 trillion. The earlier draft's broad claim that semiconductors had turned from the group's main engine into a drag was correct; the corrected version now tied that claim to Samsung's own filing rather than to secondary summaries. [Q1 2023 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2023-results>), [2023 4Q interim report](<https://images.samsung.com/is/content/samsung/assets/global/ir/docs/2023_4Q_Interim_Report.pdf>)

## Management's Tone Changed Before the Numbers Fully Did

The official language around the trough traced the mood change. In April 2023 Samsung still spoke of weak demand, inventory adjustment and a gradual second-half recovery, while also noting a roughly KRW 0.7 trillion negative operating-profit effect from the strong won. By January 2025, when it reported fiscal 2024, the company was talking about the recovery in HBM and high-density DDR5, but still warned that overall earnings improvement could remain limited because semiconductor conditions were soft in the first half of 2025. The company was therefore recovering, but not yet speaking as if the cycle had fully normalised. [Q1 2023 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2023-results>), [FY 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2024-results>)

That distinction mattered because HBM had become the industry's premium tier. Samsung said in first-quarter 2024 that it had begun 8-high HBM3E mass production and was preparing 12-high production, and by the third quarter of 2025 it said HBM3E was being sold to all related customers. But it was only in the 2026 window that the company disclosed commercial HBM4 shipment and mass-product sales of HBM4 and SOCAMM2 for NVIDIA's Vera Rubin platform. The earnings recovery therefore preceded the strongest HBM disclosures rather than depending entirely on them. [Q1 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2024-results>), [Q3 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-third-quarter-2025-results>), [HBM4 shipment](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-ships-industry-first-commercial-hbm4-with-ultimate-performance-for-ai-computing>), [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

## The Incomplete Recovery of 2024

Fiscal 2024 restored scale more quickly than confidence. Samsung returned to KRW 300.9 trillion of annual revenue and KRW 32.7 trillion of operating profit, but management still described the first half of 2025 outlook for DS as soft and emphasised technology leadership rather than immediate margin maximisation. Fourth-quarter 2024 DS operating profit was only KRW 2.9 trillion, and part of the memory improvement was being offset by higher R&D and initial ramp-up costs on cutting-edge nodes. In other words, the business had turned, but not every sub-division had yet turned cleanly with it. [FY 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2024-results>)

## The 2025-2026 Re-Acceleration

By late 2025 the earnings machine was working again at full scale. Fourth-quarter 2025 revenue reached KRW 93.8 trillion and operating profit KRW 20.1 trillion, both records at the time. Samsung also said full-year R&D investment reached KRW 37.7 trillion, a record that underlined how little the company had backed away from long-cycle spending even after the 2023 slump. [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>)

Then first-quarter 2026 revenue rose to KRW 133.9 trillion and operating profit to KRW 57.2 trillion. DS alone contributed KRW 53.7 trillion of operating profit. The move was striking not only because it set records but because it came after management had spent much of 2024 and early 2025 still speaking in cautious, bridge-year language. By the frozen window, the caution had not disappeared, but the reported numbers had moved ahead of it.

The most defensible conclusion was also the least theatrical one. Samsung's earnings story had been a memory-cycle story all along, but the quality of the recovery changed once HBM, server DRAM and enterprise SSDs took a larger share of mix. That did not erase the competitive questions around advanced-node foundry or future HBM share. It did mean the group's reported numbers by the frozen window were no longer those of a company merely climbing out of a hole; they were those of a semiconductor leader whose profit engine had restarted at unusually high intensity. [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

chapters.title: Lee Jae-yong, division leadership, and the Korean chaebol board
chapters.body:
## Succession and the Current Chain of Command

The earlier leadership chapter had become materially stale by the frozen window because it still treated Kye-hyun Kyung and Han Jong-hee as the standing co-chief executives and misassigned parts of the foundry chain. Samsung's own governance and leadership disclosures showed a different structure by May 2026. Jay Y. Lee had remained Executive Chairman since October 2022. Young Hyun Jun had taken over Device Solutions in May 2024 and was promoted in November 2025 to Vice Chairman and Chief Executive Officer while continuing to head both the DS division and the Memory business. Tae-moon Roh first became acting head of Device eXperience in April 2025 and then, in November 2025, President and CEO of Samsung Electronics while continuing to lead Mobile eXperience. [Jay Y. Lee appointment](<https://news.samsung.com/global/jay-y-lee-appointed-samsung-electronics-executive-chairman>), [DS leadership change](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-names-young-hyun-jun-as-new-head-of-device-solutions-division>), [DX leadership change](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-new-leadership-at-dx-division>), [new leadership 2025](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-new-leadership-4>)

That sequence mattered because it replaced the old co-CEO model described in the dossier with a more recent two-axis operating structure. Jun represented the semiconductor recovery and the internal demand for a more forceful DS reset after the 2023 downturn and the HBM qualification lag. Roh represented continuity on the device side, but with the remit broadened from handsets to the entire DX division just as Samsung was trying to turn Galaxy AI from a launch slogan into a product system.

## Jay Y. Lee: Formal Title After a Long De Facto Succession

Lee's formal elevation in October 2022 had been straightforwardly documented by Samsung. The significance was less the title than the closure of a prolonged transition that had begun after Lee Kun-hee's incapacitation in 2014 and continued through legal proceedings and a presidential pardon. By the frozen window, Samsung's own public architecture treated Jay Y. Lee as Executive Chairman rather than as an informal power centre waiting for formalisation. [Jay Y. Lee appointment](<https://news.samsung.com/global/jay-y-lee-appointed-samsung-electronics-executive-chairman>)

## Device Solutions: From Kye-hyun Kyung to Young Hyun Jun

Samsung announced on May 21, 2024 that Young Hyun Jun would become the new head of the Device Solutions division, while Kye-hyun Kyung moved to lead the Future Business Division and continue to head SAIT. That was the first major correction required in the chapter. The prior draft's framing of Kyung as the current DS chief executive was wrong by nearly two years relative to the frozen window. [DS leadership change](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-names-young-hyun-jun-as-new-head-of-device-solutions-division>)

The second correction was that Jun's authority expanded again in November 2025. Samsung said he had been promoted to Vice Chairman and CEO and would continue as head of Device Solutions and head of the Memory business. In practical terms, the company put the semiconductor recovery and the push to restore competitiveness in HBM and leading-edge manufacturing under one executive figure who combined divisional, business-line and corporate rank. [new leadership 2025](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-new-leadership-4>)

That leadership design also clarified a mistake in the earlier version of the dossier. Yong Kwan Kim was not the head of Foundry. Samsung's November 2024 leadership announcement named Jinman Han as President and Head of Foundry Business and Seok Woo Nam as Foundry CTO. Yong Kwan Kim, by contrast, moved into strategy-and-operations leadership inside DS and later appeared in governance materials as President & Corporate Management, Strategy & Operation for the DS Division. [new leadership 2024](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-new-leadership-3>), [Board of Directors](<https://www.samsung.com/global/ir/governance-csr/board-of-directors/>)

## Device eXperience: Roh Replaced Han at the Corporate Apex

The earlier draft also overstated Han Jong-hee's ongoing role. Samsung's 2025 half interim report said Han resigned as CEO and Executive Director on March 25, 2025. A few days later, on April 1, Samsung announced Roh as acting head of Device eXperience. Then, on November 21, 2025, the company named Roh President and CEO of Samsung Electronics and head of DX while keeping him in charge of MX. [2025 half interim report](<https://images.samsung.com/is/content/samsung/assets/global/ir/docs/2025_Half_Interim_Report.pdf>), [DX leadership change](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-new-leadership-at-dx-division>), [new leadership 2025](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-new-leadership-4>)

Roh's official board biography made the revised chain of command unusually clear. It listed him as President and CEO from 2025 onward, head of DX from 2025 onward, acting head of DX earlier in 2025, head of the Corporate Design Center from 2022 to 2025 and head of Mobile eXperience from 2020 onward. The succession on the device side therefore had not been rhetorical. It had already happened in the formal governance record. [Board of Directors](<https://www.samsung.com/global/ir/governance-csr/board-of-directors/>)

## Board and Committee Structure

As of June 30, 2025, Samsung's official half-year interim report said the board consisted of nine directors: three executive directors, Young Hyun Jun, Tae-moon Roh and Jai-Hyuk Song, and six independent directors, Je-yoon Shin, Jun-sung Kim, Eun-nyeong Heo, Myung-hee Yoo, Hye-kyung Cho and Hyuk-Jae Lee. The same report said the Management Committee consisted of the three executive directors, with Young Hyun Jun as head. [2025 half interim report](<https://images.samsung.com/is/content/samsung/assets/global/ir/docs/2025_Half_Interim_Report.pdf>)

The chair of the board was also misdated in the earlier dossier. Samsung's governance materials said the board in March 2025 appointed independent director Je-yoon Shin as chair, continuing the post-2020 practice of separating the board chair from the chief executive position. The distinction was not cosmetic. It was one of the more concrete governance changes Samsung had made in response to years of succession-related scrutiny. [FY2024 governance report](<https://images.samsung.com/is/content/samsung/assets/global/ir/docs/Corprate_Governance_Report_FY2024.pdf>), [Board committees](https://www.samsung.com/global/ir/governance-csr/board-committee/)

The board pages added one more useful correction. Jai-Hyuk Song, the finance chief, sat alongside Jun and Roh as the third executive director, which meant the current top table was not just a semiconductor-versus-device dyad. It included an explicit finance counterweight inside the executive-director group and inside the management committee architecture. [Board of Directors](<https://www.samsung.com/global/ir/governance-csr/board-of-directors/>), [Management Committee](<https://www.samsung.com/global/ir/governance-csr/board-committee/mgnt/>)

## HARMAN and the Wider Management Layer

HARMAN also needed an update. The chapter previously named the wrong chief executive. HARMAN announced in February 2025 that Christian Sobottka would become President and CEO effective April 1, 2025, succeeding Michael Mauser. By the frozen window, Samsung's automotive platform was therefore being run by Sobottka, not by the earlier management line carried in the dossier. [HARMAN CEO transition](<https://news.harman.com/releases/harman-announces-leadership-transition-christian-sobottka-appointed-as-new-president-and-chief-executive-officer>)

At the committee level, Samsung's governance pages showed that the Management Committee was composed of the executive directors, while the board biographies and committee pages placed figures such as Yong Kwan Kim in broader strategic and operational oversight roles rather than in the foundry-chief slot assigned to him in the earlier text. [Management Committee](<https://www.samsung.com/global/ir/governance-csr/board-committee/mgnt/>), [Board of Directors](<https://www.samsung.com/global/ir/governance-csr/board-of-directors/>)

## What the Corrections Changed

The independent-director bench also mattered more than the earlier draft allowed. By mid-2025 Samsung's board included Je-yoon Shin, Jun-sung Kim, Eun-nyeong Heo, Myung-hee Yoo, Hye-kyung Cho and Hyuk-Jae Lee, and the governance materials continued to emphasise committee separation and an independent chair model. That did not dissolve Samsung's succession history, but it did mean the formal oversight structure around the operating reset was stronger and more current than the stale chapter suggested. [2025 half interim report](<https://images.samsung.com/is/content/samsung/assets/global/ir/docs/2025_Half_Interim_Report.pdf>), [Board of Directors](<https://www.samsung.com/global/ir/governance-csr/board-of-directors/>)

The corrected leadership picture was less about biographical colour than about operational responsibility. By the frozen window, Samsung had put semiconductors under Young Hyun Jun, devices under Tae-moon Roh, and the board under independent chair Je-yoon Shin. Han Jong-hee and Kye-hyun Kyung were no longer current in the roles the prior draft gave them. Jinman Han, not Yong Kwan Kim, ran Foundry. Christian Sobottka, not the earlier HARMAN roster, ran the automotive subsidiary. For a company whose investment case depended heavily on execution in HBM, advanced manufacturing and AI devices, those were not cosmetic corrections; they were the current chain of command.

chapters.title: NVIDIA, hyperscalers, smartphone customers, Foundry customers, global manufacturing
chapters.body:
## NVIDIA Moved From Omission to Disclosure

The customer chapter had previously leaned on outside market-share estimates and channel talk. Samsung's own disclosures offered a firmer and, by the frozen window, more revealing sequence. In first-quarter 2024 results the company said it had started mass production of 8-high HBM3E in April and was preparing 12-high production in the second quarter. In third-quarter 2025 results it said HBM3E was in mass production and being sold to all related customers while HBM4 samples were shipping to key clients. In February 2026 Samsung announced commercial HBM4 shipment, and in first-quarter 2026 results it said it had recorded the industry's first mass-product sales of HBM4 and SOCAMM2 for NVIDIA's Vera Rubin platform. That was the primary-source basis for saying NVIDIA had become a disclosed account in the HBM4 era, even if Samsung did not publish allocation shares or contract values. [Q1 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2024-results>), [Q3 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-third-quarter-2025-results>), [HBM4 shipment](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-ships-industry-first-commercial-hbm4-with-ultimate-performance-for-ai-computing>), [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

The corrected phrasing matters. It would have been too strong to claim, from primary sources alone, that Samsung had decisively won back a lead position at NVIDIA by May 2026. It would also have been too weak to leave the dossier in its earlier state, where NVIDIA mostly appeared as an absence. Samsung itself had moved the relationship into formal disclosure.

## Cloud and Enterprise Demand Were Broad, but Mostly Undisclosed by Name

The earlier draft named hyperscalers liberally, but Samsung's own earnings releases were more careful. Through 2024, 2025 and early 2026 the company repeatedly attributed memory strength to AI and server demand, higher content per box, enterprise SSDs and high-density DDR5, without disclosing a customer ledger. That is the right level of confidence for this dossier as well. The company's most recent primary sources supported a claim of broad data-centre and enterprise exposure; they did not support a precise named-customer breakdown across Amazon, Microsoft, Google or Meta. [FY 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2024-results>), [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>), [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

What could be said with confidence was that the product mix had shifted toward the parts used most heavily in AI infrastructure. Fiscal 2025 commentary emphasised HBM, server DDR5 and enterprise SSDs. First-quarter 2026 commentary again said the Memory business would keep prioritising AI-related products. The demand signal was therefore structural enough to reshape Samsung's own planning even if the company withheld the customer roster. [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>), [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

Samsung's own technology releases supported the same pattern from the product side. LPDDR5X was being pushed beyond phones into PCs, accelerators, servers and automobiles; ninth-generation V-NAND and QLC ninth-generation V-NAND were being framed explicitly around AI-era SSD demand. That did not name the buyers, but it did show Samsung tailoring the catalog to data-centre and edge-AI use cases rather than merely waiting for demand to arrive. [LPDDR5X development](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-develops-industrys-fastest-10-7gbps-lpddr5x-dram-optimized-for-ai-applications>), [9th-gen V-NAND](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-begins-industrys-first-mass-production-of-9th-gen-v-nand>), [QLC 9th-gen V-NAND](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-begins-industrys-first-mass-production-of-qlc-9th-gen-v-nand-for-ai-era>)

## Foundry Customers: Named Wins Were Selective but Real

Where Samsung did name a customer in advanced manufacturing, the most useful frozen-window example was Preferred Networks. In July 2024 Samsung announced it would provide turnkey semiconductor solutions using its 2nm GAA process and I-Cube S 2.5D packaging to the Japanese AI company for accelerators. That release mattered because it tied together three parts of Samsung's supply-chain pitch in one deal: leading-edge process, packaging and AI end demand. [Preferred Networks](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-to-provide-turnkey-semiconductor-solutions-with-2nm-gaa-process-and-2-5d-package-to-preferred-networks>)

Samsung's broader foundry language remained more general. In the third quarter of 2025 it said the Foundry business had achieved record-high customer orders, mainly on advanced nodes. In the first quarter of 2026 it said the business would seek large-scale orders for 2nm and continue 1.4nm R&D. Those disclosures supported a narrative of improving external engagement, but not one of a fully enumerated customer book. [Q3 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-third-quarter-2025-results>), [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>), [SFF 2024](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-showcases-ai-era-vision-and-latest-foundry-technologies-at-sff-2024>)

## Internal Demand Still Mattered

Samsung's supply chain was not only external. The Galaxy handset franchise remained a major internal consumer of displays, memory and, where applicable, Exynos silicon. Samsung introduced the Galaxy S24 in January 2024 as the start of the Galaxy AI cycle and later said the S24 series had delivered double-digit full-year growth. That did not justify the earlier dossier's exact outside estimate of smartphone shipments, which was not a primary-source disclosure, but it did justify the larger point that DX still provided Samsung with a powerful internal demand anchor for premium components and industrial scale. [Galaxy S24 launch](<https://news.samsung.com/global/enter-the-new-era-of-mobile-ai-with-samsung-galaxy-s24-series>), [FY 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2024-results>)

The same was true in automotive. Samsung completed the HARMAN acquisition in 2017 and by the fourth quarter of 2025 was describing revenue growth from expanded automotive product supply to European OEMs, especially in digital cockpit and car audio. Again, the company did not publish a full OEM customer list in the earnings release, so the revised chapter avoids pretending otherwise. [HARMAN close](<https://news.samsung.com/us/samsung-electronics-completes-acquisition-of-harman>), [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>)

## Geography, Manufacturing Footprint and China Controls

Samsung's manufacturing footprint was itself part of the customer proposition. Samsung Foundry's manufacturing-sites materials described the Korea network around Giheung, Hwaseong and Pyeongtaek as the manufacturing core, while the earlier Xi'an memory project had been introduced in 2012 as a phased investment of $7 billion intended to balance Samsung's global production network. [Foundry manufacturing sites](<https://semiconductor.samsung.com/foundry/manufacturing/manufacturing-sites/>), [Xi'an groundbreaking](<https://news.samsung.com/global/groundbreaking-for-memory-manufacturing-complex-in-china>)

That footprint mattered commercially because it supported Samsung's pitch as a supply-secure partner. The company could pair massive Korean fabrication capacity with U.S. manufacturing in Austin and the coming Taylor site, and it could tie that manufacturing to its own packaging, display and device ecosystems. This is also why export-control changes mattered so much: they did not affect a marginal outpost, but part of the production web through which Samsung balanced memory supply.

The China exposure sat under a changing export-control regime. In October 2023, BIS said Samsung's PRC facilities were Validated End-Users under an updated rule covering Samsung and SK hynix. But in August 2025 BIS said it had closed the foreign-owned-fab VEU loophole, with former participants required to move to a licensing process and without approval for capacity expansion or technology upgrades in China. The earlier dossier's wording around a continuing "verified end-user" status was therefore both terminologically wrong and out of date. By the frozen window, the more accurate framing was that Samsung's China fabs had moved from VEU treatment to a tighter license regime. [BIS 2023 rule](<https://www.bis.gov/press-release/commerce-issues-rule-strengthen-national-security-partnership-secure-semiconductor-supply-chains-republic>), [BIS 2025 rule](<https://www.bis.gov/press-release/department-commerce-closes-export-controls-loophole-foreign-owned-semiconductor-fabs-china>)

## What Could Be Claimed Safely

The corrected supply-chain picture was narrower but stronger. Samsung could be tied directly, from primary sources, to NVIDIA's Vera Rubin memory stack, to a named 2nm AI foundry customer in Preferred Networks, to a large internal Galaxy demand engine and to a distinct automotive platform through HARMAN. It could also be tied to China-manufacturing exposure under a more restrictive export-control framework. What primary sources did not support was the dossier's earlier precision around HBM share, smartphone units, Xi'an output percentages or a long list of named external buyers. Those claims were pared back because the underlying source trail did not justify them.

chapters.title: Where Samsung sits against SK Hynix, TSMC, Apple, broader competitive set
chapters.body:
## Competition by Milestone, Not by Guesswork

The earlier version of this chapter relied on unsupported market-share tables. A cleaner way to compare Samsung with its closest rivals by the frozen window was to use the milestones those companies themselves had disclosed. On that basis, Samsung still looked formidable in scale but uneven in execution across the most valuable tiers of memory and foundry.

| Axis | Samsung | Key rival disclosures |
|---|---|---|
| HBM3E | Developed 36GB 12-high HBM3E in February 2024; said HBM3E was in mass production and sold to all related customers by Q3 2025 | Micron said in February 2024 it had begun volume production of HBM3E for NVIDIA H200 GPUs; Samsung's own disclosures implied it reached comparable public customer confirmation later. [Q3 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-third-quarter-2025-results>), [Micron HBM3E](<https://investors.micron.com/node/46656>) |
| HBM4 | Began commercial shipment in February 2026 and reported mass-product sales for NVIDIA Vera Rubin in Q1 2026 | Samsung's own shipment disclosure was the clearest frozen-window milestone here. [HBM4 shipment](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-ships-industry-first-commercial-hbm4-with-ultimate-performance-for-ai-computing>), [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>) |
| Leading-edge foundry | Began 3nm GAA production in June 2022; said first-generation 2nm GAA had entered mass production in Q3 2025 | TSMC said in its 2025 annual report that N2 entered high-volume manufacturing in 4Q25 with good yield; Intel said 18A was ready for customer projects and moving toward high-volume production. [Samsung 3nm](<https://news.samsung.com/us/samsung-begins-chip-production-3nm-process-gaa-architecture>), [TSMC 2025 annual report](<https://investor.tsmc.com/static/annualReports/2025/english/index.html>), [Intel 18A](<https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/foundry/process/18a.html>) |
| System solution pitch | Combined memory, foundry and advanced packaging in a single offering, exemplified by the Preferred Networks 2nm plus I-Cube S deal | TSMC's scale and customer breadth remained the benchmark, while Intel emphasised a North American process alternative. [Preferred Networks](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-to-provide-turnkey-semiconductor-solutions-with-2nm-gaa-process-and-2-5d-package-to-preferred-networks>), [TSMC 2025 annual report](<https://investor.tsmc.com/static/annualReports/2025/english/index.html>), [Intel 18A](<https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/foundry/process/18a.html>) |

## Memory: Scale Survived, Premium Timing Slipped

Primary sources did not support a precise 2024 HBM revenue-share table, but they did support the broader competitive shape. Samsung remained the largest integrated memory manufacturer by breadth, with DRAM, NAND and HBM all inside the same industrial system. Yet Micron's February 2024 announcement that it had entered HBM3E volume production for NVIDIA H200 GPUs showed that the key premium qualification race had not waited for Samsung to perfect its own program. When Samsung later said HBM3E was being sold to all related customers and then moved into commercial HBM4 shipments, it was disclosing progress from a trailing position rather than from undisputed leadership in the newest AI-memory tier. [Micron HBM3E](<https://investors.micron.com/node/46656>), [Q3 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-third-quarter-2025-results>), [HBM4 shipment](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-ships-industry-first-commercial-hbm4-with-ultimate-performance-for-ai-computing>)

That did not mean Samsung had become strategically peripheral. Its first-quarter 2026 results were the opposite: DS operating profit of KRW 53.7 trillion showed that once pricing, mix and HBM4 revenue aligned, Samsung's earnings power still exceeded that of most peers. The competitive question was more specific. Could Samsung capture the most profitable slices of the memory stack as consistently as its scale suggested it should? Through the frozen window, the answer had improved, but it was not yet definitive. [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

Samsung's advantage here was breadth. It could pair HBM with DDR5, LPDDR5X, GDDR7 and enterprise SSD supply and could use internal manufacturing scale to support customer mix shifts quickly. Its disadvantage was that the AI market cared disproportionately about the very highest-value parts, where a short delay or a narrower qualification list had outsize economic consequences. That asymmetry explains why Samsung could remain financially dominant overall while still being described, accurately, as playing catch-up in one critical memory tier.

## Foundry: First to 3nm Was Not the Same as First to Customer Confidence

Samsung's foundry position required the same distinction between technical milestone and commercial outcome. The company was genuinely first to start 3nm GAA production in June 2022. The harder point was what happened afterwards. Samsung's subsequent public messaging focused on yield improvement, customer orders, 2nm stabilisation and the combined memory-plus-packaging value proposition. That is not the language of a company that believes the node race has already been won. [Samsung 3nm](<https://news.samsung.com/us/samsung-begins-chip-production-3nm-process-gaa-architecture>), [FY 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2024-results>), [Q3 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-third-quarter-2025-results>), [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

TSMC's own primary documents illustrated the benchmark. In its 2025 annual report, TSMC said N2 had entered high-volume manufacturing in the fourth quarter of 2025 with good yield, that it had 534 customers in 2025 and that annual capacity exceeded 17 million 12-inch equivalent wafers. Those are not like-for-like metrics for Samsung's entire semiconductor complex, but they are a reminder that the foundry leader competed on both technology and customer breadth. Intel's 18A material, meanwhile, showed that Samsung was no longer contesting the advanced-node narrative with TSMC alone. [TSMC 2025 annual report](<https://investor.tsmc.com/static/annualReports/2025/english/index.html>), [Intel 18A](<https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/foundry/process/18a.html>)

Samsung's answer was integration. The Preferred Networks agreement in 2024 bundled 2nm GAA process technology with advanced 2.5D packaging. That was not just a customer announcement; it was the company's most concrete frozen-window evidence that it could sell a systems-level solution rather than merely a wafer. If Samsung narrowed the commercial gap in foundry, it was likely to do so through that combination of process, memory adjacency and packaging rather than through pure node marketing alone. [Preferred Networks](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-to-provide-turnkey-semiconductor-solutions-with-2nm-gaa-process-and-2-5d-package-to-preferred-networks>), [SFF 2024](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-showcases-ai-era-vision-and-latest-foundry-technologies-at-sff-2024>)

Samsung's manufacturing geography also influenced the comparison. Its foundry network linked Korea's Giheung, Hwaseong and Pyeongtaek sites to Austin and the planned Taylor capacity. That is not the same kind of scale claim as TSMC's 17 million 12-inch-equivalent wafers, but it does explain why Samsung kept talking about balanced manufacturing, customer proximity and system-level offerings rather than only about transistor labels. [Foundry manufacturing sites](<https://semiconductor.samsung.com/foundry/manufacturing/manufacturing-sites/>), [TSMC 2025 annual report](<https://investor.tsmc.com/static/annualReports/2025/english/index.html>)

## Devices and Automotive Still Set Samsung Apart

Where Samsung continued to look structurally different from most semiconductor peers was in the businesses wrapped around the chip stack. The Galaxy S24 launch and the later S26 AI positioning showed that Samsung still owned a major premium-device platform. HARMAN gave it a separate automotive route through digital cockpit and car audio. Neither business erased the competitive pressures in memory or foundry, but together they meant Samsung competed as a systems company rather than as a single-market specialist. [Galaxy S24 launch](<https://news.samsung.com/global/enter-the-new-era-of-mobile-ai-with-samsung-galaxy-s24-series>), [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>)

That breadth should not be romanticised. It brought managerial complexity, more moving pieces and the risk that weaker businesses could absorb capital and attention. But it also meant Samsung could offer customers and end markets something few rivals could match: components, packaging, branded devices, displays and automotive electronics inside one corporate perimeter. For some investors that breadth was a hedge. For others it was the reason the company sometimes looked slower to impose ruthless product-line focus than a more specialised peer.

The corrected competitive conclusion was therefore more nuanced than the earlier share-table version. Samsung did not need inflated or poorly sourced percentage estimates to look formidable. By the frozen window it was still one of the few groups able to compete simultaneously in advanced memory, advanced manufacturing, displays, mobile systems and automotive electronics. But the primary-source trail also showed that leadership was fragmented. Samsung still had to prove that being broad, early and heavily capitalised could consistently translate into the highest-value design wins and the stickiest AI-era allocations.

chapters.title: From 1969 founding through Lee successions, memory cycles, HBM challenge
chapters.body:
## The Next Watchpoints in the Story

By the frozen window, Samsung's near-term catalysts were less speculative than the earlier chapter made them sound. The company had already turned HBM4 into a disclosed commercial product, had moved HBM4 and SOCAMM2 into mass-product sales for NVIDIA's Vera Rubin platform, and had begun framing 2nm and device AI as the next tests of execution. The forward case therefore rested on three watchpoints management itself had identified across results releases rather than on open-ended external conjecture. [HBM4 shipment](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-ships-industry-first-commercial-hbm4-with-ultimate-performance-for-ai-computing>), [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>), [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>)

**HBM4 scale-up.** Samsung's first-quarter 2026 results said the Memory business had recorded the industry's first mass-product sales of HBM4 and SOCAMM2 for NVIDIA's Vera Rubin platform. The next catalyst was not qualification in the abstract; it was the pace at which those shipments translated into sustained revenue mix and whether HBM4 could preserve the pricing power visible in the first-quarter numbers. [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

**2nm order conversion and Taylor timing.** Samsung's third-quarter 2025 results said the Foundry business had started mass production of first-generation 2nm GAA and flagged the timely initial operation of the Taylor fab as a 2026 priority. First-quarter 2026 commentary then said the business would pursue large-scale 2nm orders while continuing 1.4nm R&D. The catalyst, in other words, was not the mere existence of a roadmap. It was commercial conversion at scale. [Q3 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-third-quarter-2025-results>), [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>), [SFF 2024](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-showcases-ai-era-vision-and-latest-foundry-technologies-at-sff-2024>)

**Galaxy AI monetisation.** Samsung launched the Galaxy S24 as the opening move in the AI-phone cycle and, by fiscal 2025, was presenting the Galaxy S26 series as the delivery vehicle for more agentic AI experiences. The watchpoint here was whether AI remained a premium-mix enhancer inside DX rather than just a marketing frame layered on top of a mature handset category. [Galaxy S24 launch](<https://news.samsung.com/global/enter-the-new-era-of-mobile-ai-with-samsung-galaxy-s24-series>), [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>)

None of those catalysts required the dossier to speculate beyond Samsung's own record. They were already present in management's disclosures; the work for investors was to track conversion from announcement to sustained economics.

chapters.title: Memory technology, Foundry advanced nodes, mobile/display IP, Bell-Labs-equivalent research
chapters.body:
## R&D as Industrial Capacity, Not Ornament

Samsung's research and development story read more cleanly in primary sources than in the earlier patent-heavy draft. The company said R&D investment reached a full-year record of KRW 37.7 trillion in 2025, and its public materials continued to describe a manufacturing and research system spanning global R&D centres, semiconductor fabs and product divisions from memory through mobile devices. The more relevant question for this dossier was not whether Samsung filed a great many patents, which it plainly did, but whether its research machine was still converting into product and process milestones that mattered commercially. [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>)

## Memory Roadmap: DRAM and NAND Milestones Were Real

On that standard, Samsung's memory R&D remained highly active. In April 2024 the company said it had developed the industry's fastest LPDDR5X DRAM at 10.7Gbps, with 25% higher performance, 30% more capacity and 25% higher power efficiency. In July 2024 it said it had completed validation of that part on MediaTek's next-generation flagship platform. Those disclosures were valuable because they located Samsung's low-power DRAM work directly in the on-device AI build-out rather than in an abstract process race. [LPDDR5X development](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-develops-industrys-fastest-10-7gbps-lpddr5x-dram-optimized-for-ai-applications>), [LPDDR5X validation](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-completes-validation-of-industrys-fastest-lpddr5x-for-use-with-mediateks-flagship-mobile-platform>)

Samsung then pushed the same family deeper into manufacturable product form. In August 2024 it said it had begun mass production of its thinnest LPDDR5X DRAM packages for on-device AI, emphasising both reduced thickness and improved heat resistance. That mattered because the company was not only racing on raw speed; it was engineering a memory stack that could fit the thermal and form-factor constraints of mobile and edge-AI devices. [LPDDR5X packages](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-begins-mass-production-of-industrys-thinnest-lpddr5x-dram-packages-for-on-device-ai>)

The NAND path was similarly specific. Samsung began mass production of ninth-generation TLC V-NAND in April 2024 and said the new part improved bit density by about 50% versus the prior generation through a double-stack structure and advanced channel-hole etching. In September 2024 it followed with mass production of QLC ninth-generation V-NAND, explicitly linking the expanded lineup to AI-era SSD demand. Those are not generic claims about innovation culture; they are dated product milestones with manufacturing consequences. [9th-gen V-NAND TLC](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-begins-industrys-first-mass-production-of-9th-gen-v-nand>), [9th-gen V-NAND QLC](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-begins-industrys-first-mass-production-of-qlc-9th-gen-v-nand-for-ai-era>)

Those product disclosures also illustrated something broader about Samsung's R&D style. The company rarely presented memory innovation as a single heroic device breakthrough. It presented it as a chain of manufacturable improvements: higher density, better thermals, better validation with platform partners and faster migration into applications beyond the original core market. That is slower to narrate than a pure design win, but it is closer to how Samsung turned process engineering into commercial advantage over long cycles.

## HBM and Advanced Packaging

The HBM path belonged in the same category. Samsung's February 2024 HBM3E 12H announcement specified up to 36GB capacity and 1,280GB per second bandwidth. Its February 2026 HBM4 shipment release specified 11.7Gbps and up to 3.3TB per second. Those figures made clear that Samsung's problem in HBM had not been a lack of product ambition or engineering throughput. It had been the translation of that work into timely commercial qualification and profitable scale. [HBM3E 12H](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-develops-industry-first-36gb-hbm3e-12h-dram>), [HBM4 shipment](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-ships-industry-first-commercial-hbm4-with-ultimate-performance-for-ai-computing>)

Samsung's packaging work also carried more commercial weight than the earlier chapter acknowledged. The Preferred Networks agreement was not just a foundry order; it attached Samsung's advanced packaging, specifically I-Cube S, to a named AI accelerator program. That is important because Samsung's differentiation in AI semiconductors increasingly rested on combining memory, logic and packaging rather than treating them as standalone businesses. [Preferred Networks](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-to-provide-turnkey-semiconductor-solutions-with-2nm-gaa-process-and-2-5d-package-to-preferred-networks>)

Samsung's results releases reinforced that reading. By the time management described HBM, server DDR5 and enterprise SSDs as the centre of the Memory business mix, the relevant R&D question was no longer whether Samsung could design ever-faster parts. It was whether the packaging, thermals, yields and validation pipeline were strong enough to move those parts quickly into the most profitable customer programs.

## Logic, Automotive and the Research Stack

In logic, Samsung's 3nm GAA announcement in June 2022 gave concrete performance claims versus 5nm: up to 45% lower power use, 23% better performance and 16% lower area in first-generation process design. By Samsung Foundry Forum 2024, the company had extended the roadmap across SF2, SF2Z and later nodes while emphasising AI-era turnkey design and ecosystem support. That made the company's research posture legible: not simply smaller transistors, but a full-stack attempt to tie process, packaging and customer enablement together. [3nm GAA production](<https://news.samsung.com/us/samsung-begins-chip-production-3nm-process-gaa-architecture>), [SFF 2024](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-showcases-ai-era-vision-and-latest-foundry-technologies-at-sff-2024>)

Samsung also pushed R&D into the automotive edge of memory and storage. In September 2024 it said it had developed the industry's first PCIe 4.0 automotive SSD based on eighth-generation V-NAND, a 256GB product designed for in-vehicle AI workloads. That did not change the centre of gravity of the company, but it showed how Samsung was trying to reuse memory and controller advances across adjacent end markets rather than keeping them confined to servers and phones. [automotive SSD AM9C1](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-develops-industrys-first-automotive-ssd-based-on-8th-generation-v-nand>)

The logic and automotive work mattered for another reason: both required Samsung to operate beyond the comfort zone of pure memory leadership. In foundry, the company needed software tools, ecosystem partners and design-service credibility. In automotive, it needed reliability, qualification and product life-cycle discipline that differed from handset cadence. The frozen-window research record showed Samsung attempting both, not merely announcing them.

## SAIT and the Long Cycle

The institutional backdrop still mattered because the research stack was not organised quarter to quarter. Samsung's public history places the opening of the Samsung Advanced Institute of Technology in 1987, and the company continues to treat SAIT as the long-horizon research hub behind nearer-cycle businesses. The revised chapter therefore stripped out weakly sourced superlatives about patent league tables and kept the facts that could be anchored in dated Samsung disclosures: record R&D spending, repeated first-in-industry memory launches, continuing gate-all-around logic work and a research apparatus still broad enough to feed all of them. [About Samsung](<https://www.samsung.com/us/about-us>)

That is a more demanding but also more useful standard for a company like Samsung. A patent count can flatter almost any large industrial group. A dated chain of product, process, validation and packaging milestones says more about whether the company is still converting research scale into economic relevance. Through the frozen window, the answer remained yes, even if the commercial reward was much larger in some domains than in others.

chapters.title: Memory cycle, HBM competition, Foundry-TSMC gap, geopolitical, chaebol governance
chapters.body:
## The Core Risk Was Still Semiconductor Concentration

Samsung's diversification softened cycles, but it did not eliminate them. The financial record itself made that clear. Operating profit fell from KRW 43.38 trillion in 2022 to KRW 6.57 trillion in 2023 before recovering to KRW 32.7 trillion in 2024 and KRW 43.6 trillion in 2025. The 2023 fourth-quarter interim report showed that DS alone lost KRW 14.8795 trillion for the full year. When the semiconductor cycle moved against Samsung, the rest of the portfolio did not come close to offsetting it. [FY 2022 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2022-results>), [FY 2023 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2023-results>), [FY 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2024-results>), [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>), [2023 4Q interim report](<https://images.samsung.com/is/content/samsung/assets/global/ir/docs/2023_4Q_Interim_Report.pdf>)

That remained the first risk for investors even after the rebound. First-quarter 2026 profits were spectacular, but they also showed how concentrated the upside had become: DS generated KRW 53.7 trillion of operating profit against only KRW 2.8 trillion for DX. The same asymmetry that created enormous earnings leverage on the way up would magnify any future deterioration in memory pricing, HBM mix or utilisation. [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

The first-quarter 2023 results also showed how fast a macro turn could hit the reported numbers. Samsung said the strong won had reduced company-wide operating profit by about KRW 0.7 trillion in that quarter, mostly in the component business. Currency therefore acted as an amplifier on top of end-demand weakness rather than as a separate nuisance variable. [Q1 2023 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2023-results>)

## HBM Execution Risk Did Not Disappear Because HBM4 Shipped

A second risk sat inside the quality of the semiconductor recovery. Samsung's own disclosures showed genuine progress: HBM3E mass production and sales to related customers by the third quarter of 2025, commercial HBM4 shipment in February 2026 and mass-product sales for NVIDIA's Vera Rubin platform in the first quarter of 2026. But those disclosures also underscored how much of the premium memory thesis now depended on staying current in a product family whose development cycle was compressing. A delay of one generation could no longer be waved away as a normal memory-cycle inconvenience. [Q3 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-third-quarter-2025-results>), [HBM4 shipment](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-ships-industry-first-commercial-hbm4-with-ultimate-performance-for-ai-computing>), [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>)

The risk was not abstract. Micron's February 2024 HBM3E volume-production announcement for NVIDIA H200 GPUs showed that alternative suppliers could move into the most profitable tier while Samsung was still working through its own commercial timeline. The earlier dossier's sourced-through-Reuters phrasing was therefore replaced with a primary-source comparison that made the same point more cleanly. [Micron HBM3E](<https://investors.micron.com/node/46656>)

## Foundry Still Required Proof, Not Just Roadmaps

Samsung Foundry remained the third major risk bucket. The company was first to begin 3nm GAA production in 2022, later said first-generation 2nm GAA had entered mass production in the third quarter of 2025 and continued to emphasise 2nm order capture and 1.4nm R&D in the first quarter of 2026. Yet management's own language made clear that commercial proof was still needed. A business that keeps highlighting large-scale order pursuit, customer wins and the timely start-up of Taylor is a business that still has milestones to clear. [Samsung 3nm](<https://news.samsung.com/us/samsung-begins-chip-production-3nm-process-gaa-architecture>), [Q3 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-third-quarter-2025-results>), [Q1 2026 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-first-quarter-2026-results>), [SFF 2024](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-showcases-ai-era-vision-and-latest-foundry-technologies-at-sff-2024>)

That risk should be read against competitors' own disclosures. TSMC said N2 had entered high-volume manufacturing in the fourth quarter of 2025 with good yield, while Intel presented 18A as ready for customer projects. Samsung did not need to beat both rivals everywhere to make Foundry worthwhile, but it did need to show that the large capital base and technological ambition could convert into durable external demand. [TSMC 2025 annual report](<https://investor.tsmc.com/static/annualReports/2025/english/index.html>), [Intel 18A](<https://www.intel.com/content/www/us/en/foundry/process/18a.html>)

## Capital Intensity and Policy Risk Stayed High

A fourth risk was the sheer weight of the investment program. Samsung's capital expenditures were KRW 53.1 trillion in 2023 and KRW 53.6 trillion in 2024, while R&D spending set a record at KRW 37.7 trillion in 2025. Those commitments were strategic strengths when end demand and pricing moved the right way. They also meant the company had less room than a fab-light peer to step away from a cycle without carrying a large fixed-cost base. [FY 2023 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2023-results>), [FY 2024 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2024-results>), [FY 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-fourth-quarter-and-fy-2025-results>)

China manufacturing exposure compounded that operating leverage. Samsung's Xi'an project began as a $7 billion phased memory investment, and the facilities remained part of the global production network. But BIS updated VEU authorisations for Samsung's PRC facilities in October 2023 and then, in August 2025, said it had closed the foreign-owned-fab VEU loophole, moving former participants onto a licensing track and signalling that capacity expansion or technology upgrades in China would not be approved. The earlier draft's continued present-tense framing of VEU treatment therefore understated the shift in policy. [Xi'an groundbreaking](<https://news.samsung.com/global/groundbreaking-for-memory-manufacturing-complex-in-china>), [BIS 2023 rule](<https://www.bis.gov/press-release/commerce-issues-rule-strengthen-national-security-partnership-secure-semiconductor-supply-chains-republic>), [BIS 2025 rule](<https://www.bis.gov/press-release/department-commerce-closes-export-controls-loophole-foreign-owned-semiconductor-fabs-china>)

Samsung's non-semiconductor businesses were not a complete hedge against those pressures. DX remained profitable, HARMAN retained automotive growth avenues and SDC still contributed earnings, but the quarter-to-quarter disclosures make clear that those businesses did not reliably offset semiconductor volatility. That matters because the existence of multiple segments can create a false sense of balance if the underlying profit distribution is not examined closely.

## Leadership Turnover Added an Execution Layer

Finally, the management reshuffle itself carried execution risk. Samsung replaced the heads of both DS and DX across 2024 and 2025, while also resetting the board chair and parts of the executive-director roster. The changes were sensible responses to the semiconductor and device cycles, but they also meant that the company entered its most important AI-cycle stretch under a recently revised leadership structure rather than under a long-settled operating team. [DS leadership change](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-names-young-hyun-jun-as-new-head-of-device-solutions-division>), [DX leadership change](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-new-leadership-at-dx-division>), [new leadership 2025](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-new-leadership-4>), [2025 half interim report](<https://images.samsung.com/is/content/samsung/assets/global/ir/docs/2025_Half_Interim_Report.pdf>)

Taylor timing also sits inside that risk bundle. Samsung itself had flagged timely initial operation of the Texas site as part of the 2026 agenda, which meant the company was balancing not only product and node execution but also industrial start-up discipline across geographies. That is not a separate thesis from HBM and foundry competitiveness; it is part of the same execution burden. [Q3 2025 results](<https://news.samsung.com/global/samsung-electronics-announces-third-quarter-2025-results>)

The corrected risk view was therefore sharper than the earlier one. Samsung did not face generic "technology competition" in the abstract. It faced a specific concentration in semiconductor earnings, a need to stay current across HBM generations, a foundry business still trying to turn milestones into customer confidence, a China manufacturing position subject to tighter export controls and a refreshed management team tasked with executing all of it at once.
